messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 39
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Airline Pilot
- Trauma Type: Police
- Pcl5: 79

He is 39 and works as an airline pilot, a job that once felt like the natural extension of who he is: disciplined, precise, calm under pressure, the kind of person others trust with their lives. He is divorced now, and in sessions he speaks with the careful, measured voice of someone who has spent years keeping himself contained. The trauma that brought him here happened during a police encounter that turned violent and chaotic in a way he still struggles to organize in his mind. What began as a routine interaction quickly became a terrifying event in which he felt trapped, exposed, and certain that he might be killed. Since then, he moves through his life as if part of him is still in that moment, waiting for the next escalation.

Before the incident, he describes himself as someone who handled stress well. Flying had taught him to stay focused when others would panic, and he took pride in being the person who could remain steady when there was trouble in the cockpit or turbulence in the air. After the police event, that confidence changes almost overnight. In the days that follow, he cannot stop replaying the scene, not as a coherent story but in fragments: the sound of voices, the sudden physical force, the feeling of being ordered to comply while his body had already gone rigid with fear. He says he keeps trying to identify the moment when things went wrong, as if understanding it perfectly might make it feel less real. Instead, the memory returns with the same sharpness each time, and he finds himself bracing before he is even aware of it.

He starts sleeping lightly, then badly. He wakes at small noises, heart pounding, already oriented toward danger. In the dark he scans the room, and if he hears footsteps in the hallway or a door close outside, his chest tightens and his mind jumps to police, sirens, shouting. At times he wakes with the sensation that someone is standing over him, and for a few seconds he cannot tell where he is. He has vivid dreams in which he is restrained or cornered, and he wakes angry, sweaty, and disoriented. The lack of sleep bleeds into everything else. He becomes quicker to irritation, more detached with his ex-wife and children, and more easily overwhelmed by ordinary problems that used to seem manageable.

At work, he is careful not to show what is happening internally. He continues flying, but he notices a constant background vigilance that never quite turns off. He checks and rechecks procedures, not because he doubts his training, but because he is desperate to stay ahead of any possibility of error or loss of control. If he sees flashing lights from the terminal or hears a stern voice over the radio, his body reacts before his mind catches up. Certain uniformed personnel at the airport can make him feel suddenly hot and unsteady. He keeps his face neutral, but internally he is counting exits, monitoring tone, and preparing himself for something he cannot name. He says he has become more aware of his own breathing, as if he is always one step away from needing to force himself to stay present.

He avoids reminders in ways that shrink his world. He changes routes when he can. He stops watching news coverage of police incidents and notices that even casual conversations about arrests or public safety make him tense. He no longer feels comfortable in crowded places where he cannot see who is approaching him. His divorce, which had already been strained, becomes harder under the weight of his withdrawal. He is physically present with family but emotionally elsewhere, often distracted, sometimes numb. He describes moments when his children are talking to him and he realizes he has not heard the last minute of conversation because his mind has drifted back to that encounter. He feels guilty about this and ashamed that he cannot simply “get over it,” especially given how much responsibility he is used to carrying for others.

Lately he says he lives with a constant sense of being on guard, as though the world is only temporarily calm. He notices himself sitting with his back to walls, watching people’s hands, listening for changes in tone. When he is triggered, he feels a surge of panic mixed with anger so intense it surprises him. He does not talk about it easily, but there is also a sadness underneath the fear: grief for the version of himself who used to feel safe, and for the trust in authority and order that no longer feels intact. Even when nothing is happening, he carries the event with him, as if his body has not yet accepted that the danger has passed.
